title: How to Choose a Multifamily Marketing Agency: 8 Questions for the Meeting
seoTitle: How to Choose a Multifamily Marketing Agency
seoDescription: Eight questions to ask any multifamily marketing agency about account ownership, fees, what counts as a lead and who checks the work.
excerpt: The capabilities deck will look fine, so these are the eight questions that show how an agency really works.
imageAlt: Regional manager and marketing director reviewing a printed report at a table in an apartment clubhouse
imageIdea: Real photo of two people reviewing a printed report in an apartment clubhouse or leasing office, candid, daylight, laptop closed, no posed handshake.
author: Michael Shad, Founder of The SocialDM
bodyHtml:
To choose a multifamily marketing agency, ask each finalist the same specific questions about account ownership, fees, what counts as a lead and who checks the work, then compare the written answers. Those answers tell you more than any capabilities deck. Every deck promises visibility. Very few explain what happens on a Tuesday when a special changes.

I run one of these agencies, so read this with that in mind. Our multifamily marketing agency page covers what we do. This post is the list I would carry into the room if I were on your side of the table.

1. Whose name is on the ad account, and who keeps it if we leave?

Ask whose card is on the Google Ads account and who holds it if the relationship ends. If a vendor owns the account, you can lose the conversion history that took months to build, and your next partner starts learning from zero. That switching cost rarely comes up in the sales meeting. It should.

2. Of our monthly budget, how much actually reached Google?

A "budget" in a vendor report is often media and fee rolled together. In one report we reviewed this year, the stated budget was about $2,690 a month. Roughly $1,550 reached Google. The rest went to the vendor. That split is not wrong on its face, but the owner should see it plainly.

You have standing to ask. Google tells advertisers they have the right to know the number of clicks, impressions and total cost of their ads, and its transparency requirements tell third party partners to report the exact amount charged by Google, separate from their fees, and to disclose the fee on customer invoices.

While you are there, ask how the fee is set. A percentage of spend pays the vendor more every time it recommends a bigger budget. We chose a flat fee for that reason, and you can weigh that as you like.

3. What do you count as a lead?

Get the definition in writing. In that same report, the month showed 14 acquisitions, all of them phone calls, because the vendor's glossary counted a call whether or not anyone answered. Property wide that month, the call log showed 29 calls, 21 missed and 4 recorded as lead calls.

The lesson there is shared. Leasing teams are on tours and can't always reach the phone, and an agency that sees a missed call pattern should raise it early and in writing, as a problem both sides own. If the definition of a lead is loose, you can be buying more calls for a phone nobody is free to answer, and nobody finds out.

4. Who on your team talks to the person running our Google profile?

Ads, social, the Google Business Profile and AI answers all reach the same renter. Ask how those people share what they learn. Ask for a recent example where something from one channel changed the work in another. A good agency answers with a story. Others answer with an org chart.

5. Who checks the work before it goes live?

Automation is fine. Automation with no reader is the risk. Google's guidance on generative AI content, updated in October 2026, says it is critical to fact check and review all AI generated content by hand before publishing, and it extends that to titles, meta descriptions and image alt text. If a vendor posts on your behalf at scale, ask who read yesterday's post and what they caught.

We think of this as the difference between an Apple Store and a warehouse club. Both can sell you the item. One has somebody accountable for what leaves the building, and that is the standard we hold ourselves to.

6. Which communities like ours have you run, and in which conditions?

A lease up and a stabilized community are different jobs, and markets differ more than most pitches admit. In September 2026, Apartment List found 57.4% of properties in Austin advertising at least a month free. In Chicago it was 1.1%. A playbook built in one of those markets may not survive the other.

Ask for anonymized examples if they cannot name clients. Plenty of agencies protect client names, ours included, so silence on names is not a red flag. Silence on specifics is.

7. What will your report tell me to do on Monday?

Request a real sample with the names removed. Then look for three things: the date of each number, what changed since last time, and one decision the report is asking you to make. Multifamily teams are not short on data, as we argued in our post on the discovery problem. They are short on someone reading it for them.

If impressions went up and nothing says what that did for tours, press on it. Also check whether the report ever admits something did not work. One that never does is a sales document.

8. What can't you promise?

Google's own advice on hiring help is blunt: "No one can guarantee a #1 ranking on Google." It adds that if someone guarantees first place, "find someone else." Google also suggests asking "What kind of results do you expect to see, and in what timeframe?"

A strong answer names what the agency controls, what it influences and what depends on your site platform, your onsite team or the market. I would be cautious of anyone who has no list.

Does price per door tell you anything?

It tells you how a vendor bills. It does not tell you what is included, who does it or how often anyone looks at your community. Two proposals at the same per door figure can differ by a whole service line. Line the scopes up first, price second.

How should you score the answers?

Send the same questions to every finalist and ask for written replies. Watch how long each one takes and how specific it gets. Vague answers at the sales stage seldom sharpen after the contract is signed. Then ask to speak with a current client who has been through a hard month, since that call will tell you how the agency behaves when results dip. If you want to put these questions to us, start with the LocalLift page.

Questions we hear

Should we hire one agency or several specialists?

Either can work. What matters is that one person owns the facts and the plan for each community. Several specialists with no owner is usually where renters start seeing conflicting information.

What should a multifamily marketing agency cost?

Scope varies too much for one honest number. Compare what is included, what goes to media versus fees, and whether the fee grows when your budget does.

Is it a red flag if an agency will not name clients?

Not by itself. Many agencies protect client names. Ask for anonymized examples with real specifics instead, and for a reference call.

How soon can we judge a new agency?

Ask each one for its timeline up front, and hold it to that. Early signs are clean accounts, accurate facts and clear reporting, and those show up well before leases do.

Do we need an agency if listing sites already send us leads?

Listing sites are a major source for renters, and they are worth keeping. The question is how much you depend on them, which we cover in why communities need more than ILS leads.
